summary: Describes the SURVEY program at MIT-DMCG that regularly tried connecting to hosts to record whether they were reachable and how fast they responded, and reports the results of its first months. It invites corrections to the data.

plainLanguage.summary: A robot kept knocking on every computer's door every fifteen minutes to see who answered, and here are its notes.

questions: how was arpanet host uptime measured
subtitle: The MIT-DMCG SURVEY program, which knocked on every ARPANET host every 15 minutes to see who was answering.

tldr.problem: Users and implementers had no regular record of which ARPANET hosts were reachable or how quickly they responded.
tldr.mechanism: A SURVEY program on the MIT-DMCG ITS PDP-10 tries a connection to the LOGGER (socket 1) of each listed host every 15 minutes and records one of five statuses and the response time.
tldr.outcome: The RFC reports the first months of data and admits its limits, such as counting scheduled downtime against hosts. The unit metadata lists RFC 530 as an update to it.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 530 as an update to this report and gives its status as unknown. The data is a snapshot from December 1971 to March 1972.

sections.title: The SURVEY Program
sections.content:
Several months before this March 1972 note, a SURVEY program was implemented on the MIT-DMCG ITS PDP-10 to gather information on host availability. The RFC has three aims: announce the service and how to reach it, present the first few months of results, and correct errors in the data or methods.

Whenever the ITS time-sharing system is in normal operation, a survey starts at 15-minute intervals. It tries to connect to the LOGGER (socket 1) of each host in its table and records the result. The Initial Connection Protocol is aborted before the socket number is read, to cause the least processing at the surveyed hosts. If the connection succeeds, the host's average response time, in seconds, is updated.
sections.plainLanguage: Every fifteen minutes the robot rings each computer's doorbell and runs away before anyone opens, just to see if someone is home and how fast they come.

sections.title: The Five Statuses and the Commands
sections.content:
Each test ends in one of five statuses: LOGGER available (connection completed), LOGGER not responding (RFC sent but no response in 20 seconds), LOGGER rejecting (CLOSE returned by the NCP), NCP not responding (RESET timed out after 15 seconds) and HOST dead (host-dead status returned by the IMP).

To see the data, follow the scenario in RFC 254 and reach NETWRK, the DMCG user Telnet. Seven commands relate to survey data, including SUMMARY.OF.SURVEYS, HISTORY.OF., ACTIVE.HOSTS, BEST.SURVEY and long-term versions covering everything since December 13, 1971. Recent means within the last 24 hours or less.
sections.plainLanguage: The robot writes one of five notes for each knock: someone answered, nobody answered, the door was slammed, the whole house was not listening, or the street was empty.

sections.title: Results and Their Limits
sections.content:
The table covers 6528 surveys from 09:55:18 on 12/13/71 to 08:50:41 on 03/20/72, listing each host's percentage up and average response. Examples include ucla-ccn at 070% and mit-dmcg at 093%; several hosts show 000%.

The authors name shortcomings. SURVEY only runs when the MIT-DMCG system and its IMP are up, so the 94% figure for MIT-DMCG is inaccurate and should be closer to 66%. It runs around the clock and ignores advertised uptime, so MIT-DMCG can never exceed 67% on a Tuesday. And the Lincoln Lab TX-2 shows as never available because of an undiagnosed problem under investigation. Here, up means that the Logger is accepting connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The robot's chart has mistakes it admits to: it only works when its own house has power, and it counts times when computers were announced to be closed.
